prompt: A tank endorsement is needed for tanks with an individual rated capacity of more than how many gallons (when the total is 1,000 gallons or more)?
choices: 119 gallons
500 gallons
99 gallons
250 gallons
explanation: A tank vehicle carries liquid or gas in tanks with an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more.

prompt: What total (aggregate) tank capacity makes a vehicle a tank vehicle, if each tank holds more than 119 gallons?
choices: 500 gallons or more
1,000 gallons or more
2,000 gallons or more
Over 3,500 gallons
explanation: The aggregate rated capacity must be 1,000 gallons or more, with each tank over 119 gallons.

prompt: Does the liquid in a tank have to be hazardous for a tank endorsement to be required?
choices: Only if the vehicle is placarded
Yes, only liquids listed as hazardous materials count
No, any liquid or gas in qualifying tanks counts
Yes, only flammable liquids count
explanation: The liquid or gas does not have to be a hazardous material. Water, milk and other non-hazardous liquids hauled in qualifying tanks still require the endorsement.

prompt: Which letter code is used for the tank vehicle endorsement?
choices: T
H
X
N
explanation: The tank vehicle endorsement is N. T is doubles/triples, H is hazardous materials, and X is the combined tank and hazmat endorsement.

prompt: A driver hauls gasoline in a tank vehicle in amounts that require placards. Which endorsement shows both required qualifications?
choices: H
X
T
N
explanation: Drivers of tank vehicles hauling hazardous materials in amounts requiring placards need both tank and hazmat qualifications, shown by the X endorsement.
ref: CDL Manual, Section 1 (CDL Endorsements & Restrictions); 49 CFR 383.93

prompt: A Class B straight truck has a single 900-gallon tank of drinking water. Does the driver need a tank endorsement?
choices: No, the total capacity is under 1,000 gallons
Yes, all water trucks need it
Yes, because any single tank over 119 gallons needs it
Only if the tank is temporarily attached
explanation: The rule requires each tank to be over 119 gallons AND a total of 1,000 gallons or more. A single 900-gallon tank does not reach 1,000 gallons.

prompt: A Class B truck carries two permanently mounted 600-gallon tanks of water. Does the driver need a tank endorsement?
choices: No, because the tanks are permanently mounted
No, because water is not a hazardous material
Yes, each tank is over 119 gallons and the total is 1,200
No, because neither tank alone holds 1,000 gallons or more
explanation: Each tank is over 119 gallons and the total is 1,000 gallons or more, so this is a tank vehicle. The liquid does not need to be hazardous.

prompt: A Class A rig carries ten 110-gallon tanks of liquid, 1,100 gallons in all. Under the federal definition, is it a tank vehicle?
choices: Yes, because the combined capacity is more than 1,000 gallons
Only if the liquid is hazardous
Yes, because there are more than five tanks
No, because no single tank holds more than 119 gallons
explanation: Both parts must be met: each tank over 119 gallons and a total of 1,000 gallons or more. Tanks of 110 gallons each do not meet the individual capacity part.

prompt: Does a tank temporarily attached to a vehicle count toward the tank endorsement rule?
choices: Yes, tanks permanently or temporarily attached both count
Only if it is bolted to the frame
Only if it is attached for more than 30 days
No, only tanks that are permanently attached to the chassis count
explanation: The rule covers tanks that are either permanently or temporarily attached to the vehicle or chassis.

prompt: A flatbed is hauling an empty 1,500-gallon storage tank that is not designed for transporting cargo. Under federal rules, is this a tank vehicle?
choices: Yes, because it is temporarily attached
Yes, any tank of 1,000 gallons or more counts
Only if it last held a hazardous liquid
No, an empty storage tank not designed for transport is excluded
explanation: Federal rules state that a CMV carrying an empty storage container tank not designed for transportation, temporarily attached to a flatbed, is not a tank vehicle.

prompt: When does a Class C vehicle require a tank endorsement?
choices: Never; the tank rules cover only Class A or Class B vehicles
When it has more than one axle
When it carries hazardous materials in liquid or gas form in qualifying tanks
Whenever it carries any liquid
explanation: A tank endorsement applies to Class A and B vehicles hauling qualifying tanks of any liquid or gas, and to Class C vehicles only when they transport hazardous materials in liquid or gas form in such tanks.

prompt: A commercial learner's permit holder has an N endorsement. What may they drive under the X restriction?
choices: Any tank vehicle on private roads
Only an empty tank vehicle, purged if it held hazmat
Only a loaded tank under 1,000 gallons
Any tank vehicle, as long as a CDL holder rides along
explanation: A CLP with an N endorsement carries an X restriction: the holder may only operate an empty tank vehicle, and not one that previously held hazmat unless it has been purged of any residue.

prompt: Why do bulk liquids cause driving control problems?
choices: Liquids weigh less than dry freight of the same volume
Liquids make the steering feel lighter at low speeds
The cargo is heavy, shifts easily, and rides high
Tank trailers have no brakes on the rear axle
explanation: Liquids in bulk are heavy, prone to shifting, and have a high center of gravity, which is why tank drivers must pass a special knowledge test.

prompt: When should you inspect a tank vehicle?
choices: Only when a leak is reported
Only after unloading, once the tank is empty and safe to enter
Only once a week
Before loading, unloading, or driving it
explanation: Before loading, unloading or driving a tanker, inspect the vehicle to make sure it is safe to carry the liquid or gas and safe to drive.

prompt: Where should you look to learn how to inspect your particular tank vehicle?
choices: The vehicle's operator manual
The shipping paper
The state driver handbook
The tank's capacity plate only
explanation: Tank vehicles come in many types and sizes. Check the vehicle's operator manual to make sure you know how to inspect your tank vehicle.

prompt: On all tank vehicles, what is the most important item to check?
choices: Tire tread depth
Leaks
Mirror adjustment
Fuel level
explanation: On all tank vehicles, the most important item to check for is leaks. Check under and around the vehicle for any sign of leaking.

prompt: What can happen if you haul liquid in a tank you know is leaking?
choices: You get a warning the first time
You can be cited, stopped from driving, and held liable for cleanup
Nothing, as long as the leak is small and the liquid is not hazardous
You only need to report it at the end of the trip
explanation: Carrying liquids or gases in a leaking tank is a crime. You will be cited and prevented from driving further, and you may be liable for cleaning up any spill.

prompt: During inspection, what should you check about the intake, discharge and cut-off valves?
choices: That they are all fully open before the vehicle is moved to the loading rack
That they are greased weekly
That they are painted the right color
That each is in the correct position before loading, unloading or moving
explanation: Check the intake, discharge and cut-off valves and make sure they are in the correct position before loading, unloading or moving the vehicle.

prompt: Where are leaks in pipes, connections and hoses most likely to be found?
choices: Around the joints
On the top of the tank
In the middle of straight pipe runs
explanation: Check pipes, connections and hoses for leaks, especially around joints.

prompt: What should you check on the manhole covers and vents of a tank?
choices: Vents are plugged to stop spills
Covers are painted to match the tank
Covers have gaskets and close right, and vents are clear
Covers are left slightly loose so the tank can breathe
explanation: Make sure manhole covers have gaskets and close correctly, and keep the vents clear so they work correctly.

prompt: Which of these is special purpose equipment you should make sure works on a tank vehicle?
choices: Cab marker lights
Mud flaps
Sleeper berth curtains and bunk restraints
Grounding and bonding cables
explanation: If your tank has them, make sure vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems and built-in fire extinguishers work.

prompt: Is it ever acceptable to drive a tank vehicle with a manhole cover open?
choices: Yes, when the tank is empty
No, never drive with open valves or manhole covers
Yes, to vent fumes in hot weather
Yes, for short moves inside a terminal or loading yard
explanation: Never drive a tank vehicle with open valves or manhole covers.

prompt: What should you do about the emergency equipment for your tank vehicle?
choices: Leave it at the terminal to keep the vehicle under weight limits
Rely on the shipper to carry it
Find out what is required and make sure it is there and works
Check it only once a year
explanation: Check the emergency equipment required for your vehicle: find out what you must carry and make sure you have it and it works.

prompt: What two factors make hauling liquids in tanks require special skills?
choices: A high center of gravity and liquid movement
Heavy steering and weak brakes
Short wheelbase and small mirrors
Low ground clearance and a wider turning path than other trucks
explanation: Hauling liquids requires special skills because of the high center of gravity and the movement of the liquid (surge).

prompt: What does a high center of gravity mean for a tank vehicle?
choices: The brakes must work harder going uphill
Much of the load's weight is high off the road, so it tips easily
The tank sits low and can scrape on steep ramps and driveways
The truck is hard to steer at slow speeds
explanation: A high center of gravity means much of the weight is carried high up off the road. This makes the vehicle top-heavy and easy to roll over.

prompt: How fast should a liquid tanker take highway curves and on- and off-ramps?
choices: Well below the posted speed
Slightly above the posted speed
At the posted speed
At the same speed as other traffic
explanation: Tests have shown tankers can turn over at the speed limits posted for curves. Take curves and ramps well below the posted speeds.

prompt: What is liquid surge?
choices: A sudden rise in pressure inside the tank
Liquid expanding as it warms up during the trip
Movement of liquid in a partly filled tank
Liquid leaking out of a vent
explanation: Liquid surge results from movement of the liquid in partially filled tanks, and it can have bad effects on handling. Liquid expanding as it warms is the reason for outage.

prompt: When a partially loaded tanker comes to a stop, what does the surge tend to do?
choices: Lock the trailer brakes
Lift the front wheels off the road
Pull the truck back toward where the stop began
Push the truck in the direction the wave is moving
explanation: When stopping, the liquid surges back and forth. When the wave hits the end of the tank, it tends to push the truck in the direction the wave is moving.

prompt: You stop a partially loaded tanker at an intersection on an icy road. What hazard should you expect?
choices: The brakes will release on their own after a few seconds
The surge can push the stopped truck into the intersection
The tank will lose pressure
The liquid will freeze and stop moving
explanation: On a slippery surface such as ice, the surge wave can shove a stopped truck out into an intersection.

prompt: What do bulkheads do in a liquid tank?
choices: Hold the tank onto the frame
Keep the liquid cool
Let liquid flow through holes between sections
Divide the tank into several smaller tanks
explanation: Bulkheads divide a liquid tank into several smaller tanks. Baffles are bulkheads with holes that let liquid flow through.

prompt: When loading or unloading the compartments of a tank divided by bulkheads, what must the driver watch?
choices: Only the total number of gallons loaded into the whole tank
The color of each liquid
Weight distribution, so the front or rear is not overloaded
The order in which the hoses are coiled
explanation: When loading and unloading the smaller tanks, pay attention to weight distribution. Don't put too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle.

prompt: You deliver from the rear compartment of a bulkhead tank first, leaving the front compartments full. What should concern you?
choices: Too much weight may be left on the front of the vehicle
The tank will need a new outage setting
Nothing, the order does not matter
Surge will become stronger in the empty rear compartment
explanation: With bulkhead tanks, watch weight distribution as compartments are loaded and unloaded, and don't put too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle.

prompt: How are baffles different from solid bulkheads?
choices: Baffles are only found in smooth bore tanks
Baffles have holes that let liquid flow through
Baffles stop all side-to-side surge
Baffles completely seal off each section
explanation: Baffled tanks have bulkheads with holes that let the liquid flow through, which helps control forward and backward surge.

prompt: Baffles help control forward-and-back surge. What kind of surge can still occur in a baffled tank?
choices: Only surge when the tank is full
No surge at all once the baffles are installed
Side-to-side surge, which can cause a rollover
Only up-and-down surge
explanation: Baffles help control forward and backward surge, but side-to-side surge can still occur, and it can cause a rollover.

prompt: What is a smooth bore tank?
choices: A tank divided by solid bulkheads
A tank lined to resist corrosion
A tank with baffles that have smooth, rounded edges
A tank with nothing inside to slow the liquid
explanation: Un-baffled liquid tanks, sometimes called smooth bore tanks, have nothing inside to slow the flow of the liquid, so forward-and-back surge is very strong.

prompt: Which type of cargo is usually hauled in smooth bore tanks?
choices: Food products such as milk
Only placarded hazardous materials
Only liquids too thick to surge
Only compressed gases under pressure
explanation: Un-baffled (smooth bore) tanks are usually those that transport food products, such as milk, because sanitation rules forbid baffles that are hard to clean.

prompt: Why are baffles not used in tanks that haul milk?
choices: Milk tanks are always filled completely to the top
Milk is too thick to surge
Baffles would change the milk's taste
Sanitation rules forbid them because cleaning is hard
explanation: Sanitation regulations forbid baffles in food tanks because of the difficulty of cleaning the inside of the tank.

prompt: When is a smooth bore tank most difficult to handle?
choices: When starting and stopping
When cruising at a steady speed
When parked on level ground
When the tank is completely empty
explanation: Forward-and-back surge is very strong in smooth bore tanks. Be extremely cautious (slow and careful), especially when starting and stopping.

prompt: What is outage?
choices: Liquid lost through a leaking valve or loose fitting
The amount of liquid left after unloading
Room left in a tank for the liquid to expand
The time a tank is out of service
explanation: Never load a cargo tank totally full. Liquids expand as they warm, and the room left for expansion is called outage.

prompt: Do all liquids need the same amount of outage?
choices: Yes, always one foot below the top
No, different liquids expand by different amounts
Only heated liquids need outage
Yes, it is always 10 percent of the tank's capacity
explanation: Different liquids expand by different amounts, so they require different amounts of outage. You must know the outage requirement for what you haul.

prompt: Why might you only partly fill a tank with a dense liquid, such as some acids?
choices: A full tank could go over legal weight limits
Dense liquids cannot surge
Partial loads are easier to unload
Dense liquids do not expand when they warm up
explanation: A full tank of dense liquid may exceed legal weight limits, so tanks hauling heavy liquids are often only partly filled.

prompt: Which of these helps determine how much liquid you can load into a tank?
choices: The time of day of delivery
The number of delivery stops planned on the route
How much the liquid will expand in transit
The fuel level of the tractor
explanation: The amount to load depends on how much the liquid will expand in transit, the weight of the liquid, and legal weight limits.

prompt: Because of the high center of gravity and surge, how should a tank vehicle be driven?
choices: Change lanes quickly to limit time beside other vehicles
Start, slow down, stop, turn, and change lanes very smoothly
Accelerate quickly to get ahead of the surge
Brake hard and early to settle the liquid
explanation: You must start, slow down and stop very smoothly, and make smooth turns and lane changes.

prompt: How should you use the brakes to control surge when stopping a tanker?
choices: Pump the brakes rapidly all the way to the stop
Use only the trailer hand valve
Release the brakes just before the truck stops
Keep steady pressure and don't release too soon
explanation: Keep a steady pressure on the brakes and do not release too soon when coming to a stop.

prompt: To help control surge, what should you do about stopping and following distance?
choices: Coast to every stop without using the brakes at all
Follow closely so you can brake gently
Brake late and keep your normal following distance
Brake early and increase your following distance
explanation: Brake far in advance of a stop and increase your following distance.

prompt: You must make a quick stop in a tanker to avoid a crash. Which braking method should you use?
choices: Controlled or stab braking
Pump the brakes gently
Hold the pedal down as hard as possible
Use only the parking brake
explanation: If you must make a quick stop, use controlled or stab braking. Jamming on the brakes locks the wheels and causes a skid.

prompt: What is controlled braking?
choices: Pumping the pedal lightly
Braking fully, then releasing each time the wheels lock up
Braking as hard as you can without locking the wheels
Braking only with the trailer brakes
explanation: With controlled braking you apply the brakes as hard as you can without locking the wheels, keeping steering movements very small.

prompt: When stab braking, why must you wait for the wheels to start rolling before braking again?
choices: The air tanks need time to refill
If you reapply too soon, the vehicle won't straighten out
The brake drums need time to cool
The surge must stop first
explanation: It can take up to one second for the wheels to start rolling after you release. If you reapply before they roll, the vehicle won't straighten out.

prompt: You are braking hard in a loaded tanker and swerve sharply. What is the main danger?
choices: The trailer will lift off the fifth wheel
The liquid will begin to foam
The tank vents will open
The vehicle may roll over
explanation: If you steer quickly while braking, a tank vehicle may roll over.

prompt: What is the correct way to take a curve in a tank vehicle?
choices: Slow down before the curve, then speed up slightly in it
Coast through the curve in neutral
Brake steadily all the way through the curve until the exit
Enter at the posted speed and brake if needed
explanation: Slow down before curves, then accelerate slightly through the curve. The posted speed for a curve may be too fast for a tank vehicle.

prompt: How do wet roads affect stopping distance?
choices: They have no effect on a heavy tanker
They can double the normal stopping distance
They add about 10 percent
They cut it in half because of the weight
explanation: Wet roads double the normal stopping distance.

prompt: Compared with a loaded tank vehicle, an empty one:
choices: Stops in exactly the same distance
Cannot skid
May take longer to stop
Always stops in a shorter distance
explanation: Empty tank vehicles may take longer to stop than full ones. Don't assume an empty tanker stops shorter.

prompt: What driver actions can cause a tank vehicle to skid?
choices: Driving at a steady speed below the limit
Using the engine brake on dry, level roads
Keeping a long following distance
Over-steering, over-accelerating, or over-braking
explanation: Don't over-steer, over-accelerate or over-brake. If you do, your vehicle may skid.

prompt: On a tank trailer, the drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid. What may happen?
choices: The trailer brakes will release
The tank will automatically vent
The vehicle may jackknife
The liquid will stop surging
explanation: On tank trailers, if the drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid, the vehicle may jackknife.

prompt: When any vehicle starts to skid, what must you do?
choices: Shift into a higher gear
Take action to restore traction to the wheels
Brake harder to stop the skid
Turn the wheel sharply the other way
explanation: When any vehicle starts to skid, you must take action to restore traction to the wheels.
